full_judgment:
2. The opposite parties as plaintiffs have instituted a Title Suit being Title Suit No. 16 of 1993 in the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Rupganj under the District of Narayangonj for permanent injunction against the petitioners and the defendant- respondent opposite party Nos. 7 to 9. The further case of the plaintiff is that, one Akbar Bhuiyan was the owner of CS Khatian No. 15 with other land and Jonab Ali and others were the owners of the CS Khatian No. 243 including the disputed land and also other land. Before CS operation the CS Plot of CS Khatian No. 15 was owned and possessed by one Maizuddin and after a few years the said Maizuddin handed over the possession of the said Khatian to Akbar Bhuiyan. Thereafter, the whole of the CS Khatian Nos. 15 and 243 was sold out on auction and the said auction was purchased by the landlord Asliutosh Bandopadhaya and others. Thereafter, the said properties including the disputed properties were handed over to one Mohabbat Khan and the possession of the said properties was also given to him before 1940 and thus Mohabbat Khan became the owner and peaceful possessor of the said disputed land including other land by paying rent to the then Zaminder, Babu Ashutosh Bandopadhaya and others. Mohabbat Khan died leaving behind his three sons namely, Ayer Khan, Taiub Khan and Ala Box and the SA and RS parcha were prepared in the name of Ayer Khan, Taub Khan and Ala Box correctly and thereafter Ayer Khan died leaving behind two sons namely, Karim Khan, Salamat Khan and one daughter Tamarun Nessa and wife Sakhina, the opposite party Nos. 1-3 and 6 as his legal heirs and thus the plaintiff-appellant-opposite party Nos. 1 to 6 have been owning and possessing the suit land for more than 50 years within the knowledge of everybody including the defendant- respondents-petitioners and the plaintiff-opposite parties have been owning and peacefully possessing the suit land by growing seasonal crops and the defendant-petitioners have no interest and possession over the suit land including the schedule land. The defendant-petitioners with the malafide intention and to grab the properties tried to dispossess the plaintiff-opposite parties on 19-3-1993 from 9-00 to 10-00 AM but with the intervention of the local people the plaintiff opposite parties were saved from dispossession of the suit land. The plaintiff-opposite parties are compelled to file the suit for permanent injunction. 

 3. The case of the defendant-respondent- petitioners are that, one Akbar Ali Bhuiyan was the owner and possessor of CS Khatian No. 15. Janab Ali and others were the 16 annas owners and possessors of CS Khatian No. 243 and thereafter, Akbar Bhuiyan and Janab Ali and others handed over the possession of the said properties of Khatian Nos. 15 and 243 to one Maizuddin and Jasar Ali through Dao Sidda Bandak, thereafter the said properties were sold out on auction for want of rent. Thereafter, the father of Mahabbat Khan and Ismat Khan, that is Suja Khan, purchased the said sale of auction from the then Zaminder. Thereafter, Suja Khan and Ismat Khan died leaving behind two sons namely, Mohabbat Khan and Ismat Khan as his legal heirs and on amicable partition the disputed land has fallen in a saham of Ismat Khan and as a result he had been owning and possessing the said land. The RS parcha was prepared in the name of Ismat Khan and Mohabbat Khan correctly though the name of Ismat Khan shown in the RS Parcha as eight annas share and Mohabbat Khan also got eight annas share by amicable partition. Son of Mohabbat Khan had been owning and possessing the said land. Thereafter Ismat Khan sold out 0.45 acres of land out of 0.50 acres to Kala Chand from the plot No. 360 on 5-12-1997 vide registered Deed No. 35286 and handed over peaceful possession of the said land Ismat Khan also sold out 30 acres of land out of 36 acres from plot No. 361 on 12-3-1979 vide registered Deed No. 792 to one Mr Kala Chand, the petitioner No.1, and also handed over peaceful possession of the said plot. Thereafter Ismat Khan gifted the 0.04½ acres of land from plot No. 360 to his grandsons, Serajul Islam Khan and Md Dulal Khan on 12-3-1979 vide Registered Deed No. 795 and handed over the possession of the said land to his aforesaid grandsons. Thereafter, the rest portion i.e. 0.04-1/2 acres of land from plot No. 360. The disputed property was also gifted to his son Rup Chand on 12-3-1979 vide Registered Deed No. 794. Thereafter the said Rouf Khan, Serajul Islam Khan and the mother of Dulal Khan, Tara Bhanu sold out their 0.09 acres of land of plot No. 36 and 0.06 acres of land from plot No. 361 to Kala Chand on 27-8-1980 vide Registered Sub- Kabala deed being No. 794 and thus, this Kala Chand became the absolute owner and possessor of 0.54 acres of land from plot No. 360 and 0.36 acres of land from plot No. 361 for long more than 12 years and this Kala Chand mutated his name in separate Khatian and has been owning and possessing the schedule land by paying rents to the Government regularly. The plaintiff opposite parties have no right, title, possession and interest over the suit land in any manner and the claim of the plaintiff-appellant is false and a fabricated story and no occasion or occurrence took place. The plaintiff-opposite party have no right, title, interest and possession over an inch of the suit land. The defendant-petitioners are in possession of the suit land by way of cultivating the land and by recting houses over some portion of the schedule land. The plaintiff-opposite parties are not entitled to get decree of the suit land. The defendant-petitioner also stated in the written statement that while they were coming back from the Chamber of their learned Advocate of Upazila Court of Rupganj they lost the original deed including other valuable deeds on the way to their residence and they have filed a GD in the concerned thana, they are the owners and possessors of the entire suit land except 0.03 acres of land as the said 0.03 acres of land was acquired by the C&B Department for road. 

 4. The defendant-respondent-opposite party Nos. 7 to 9 also have filed written statement to the effect that they have been owning and possession the 0.54 acres of land from plot No. 360 by growing seasonal crops and they got the properties from the predecessors by way of inheritance and they have appointed one Md Moser Ali as their Attorney for maintenance of their property amounting to 3.23 acres of land including 0.52 acres of the suit land. But their names were not recorded in the SA Khatian for which they have filed another suit for declaration of title being Title Suit No. 54 of 1993 in the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Rupganj against the plaintiffs-appellant-respondent-opposite party and while this defendant-opposite party petitioner No. 1 came to know that suit for declaration has started this defendant-petitioner filed a petition under Order I rule 10 for adding them as party in the aforesaid suit and the learned court was pleased to add them as party in that suit being Title Suit No. 54 of 1993. After conclusion of the trial the learned Court was pleased to dismiss the suit on contest and plaintiff filed an appeal against the said judgment and decree which is now pending before the court of Additional District Judge. 

 7. Mr Probir Halder, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant- opposite parties, submits that though the pattan was not produced by the plaintiff but it is admitted fact that SA was prepared in the name of the sons of Mohabbat Khan, predecessor of the plaintiff, but name of the predecessor of the defendant has never been entered in the SA Khatian. Therefore, the chain of ownership could not be established and subsequent registration of documents; therefore does not create any title or ownership in the name of the defendant-petitioner and he has referred 2 BLC (AD) 92 that the High Court Division has no jurisdiction to disturb the final findings of facts on the ground mentioned in section 115 of the CPC without reversing the findings of the courts below and it cannot superimpose itself as a third Court for fresh application of evidence which is not its function and thereby it exceeded its revisional jurisdiction" and also referred in the same 2 BLC 134 (AD) Concurrent finding of fact. It cannot be sa.id that a finding of fact whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the lower appellate Court is binding on the High Court, as a revisional Court except in certain well-defined exceptional circumstances such :3.S non-consideration or misreading of material evidence affecting the merit of the case. Besides, the oral evidence the sale deeds and the SA Khatian on the basis of which the rents were alleged to have been paid by the plaintiffs though rent receipts have been duly considered by the appellate Court which is the final court of fact, the High Court Division was not correct in reversing the concurrent decisions of the Courts below." In this context he submits that the appellate Court has considered the dakhilas and the rent receipts Exhibits 6 and 5 from where it is established that the plaintiff-opposite party are in possession and title of the disputed property and further submits that as per schedule of the plaint, it has been specifically mentioned the total land which the plaintiff requires and sought for injunction thereby the suit plot is specifically demarcated and he is entitled to have injunction and submits that the registered deed by which the petitioner is claiming the property has got no basis as the petitioner could not establish the chain of ownership in the disputed property. Mr Halder further refers that though the petitioner was paying rent up to 1991, under a mutation case No. 174 of 1974 of 1986 that mutation case was dismissed against which the defendant preferred appeal and the appeal is pending before the learned ADC (Rev). Therefore though the petitioner has paid rent still they have not acquired any title in the disputed property. 

 8. I have gone through the judgments of both the courts below and also Exhibits as filed by both the parties. Admitted fact is that the CS Khatian was prepared in the name of Jagadish and Ashutosh from where the plaintiff claims the ownership but the pattans were not produced by plaintiff and defendant before the court though RS was prepared in the name of the predecessor of the plaintiff and defendants. The plaintiff produced some dakhilas and also rent receipts i.e. Exhibit 5 which appeared to have been paid on 16-3-1980 and Exhibit 5 Ka is paid in 1969 in the name of Tayab Khan and Exhibit 6 series are the dakhilas given by the jaminder and the defendants have also filed rent receipts of the government which were marked as Exhibit A series and admitted position is that he paid rent up to 1991. The defendants have mutated and submitted some documents of that purchase deed of different dates i.e. 12-3-1979 and 5-12-1979. The dakhilas submitted by the plaintiff are the private documents and that are ie, to be proved by the scribe, the signatures are to be compared which were not considered by the lower appellate Court. These private dakhilas are yet to be proved and it is referred in 35 DLR 129 "that dakhilas are private documents and it would not carry any presumption of correctness as would be available in the case of any entry in the record of rights under the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act. It appears that both the parties have adduced rent receipts and the petitioner has paid rent up to 1991 and there was mutation though the mutation proceeding is under challenge in the appeal and, according to decision 35 DLR (AD) 216, rent receipts are evidence of possession, and may be used as collateral evidence of title. The petitioner has submitted certain rent receipts marked as Exhibit A series which were not considered by the learned appellate Court. Though it is a question of fact based on finding and is proved and this aspect since not discussed by the learned appellate Court, I find substance in this Rule. Since rent receipts are evidence of possession and collateral evidence of title and in a suit for permanent injunction where the plaintiff did not mention the boundary of the specific plot and there is no specific demarcation, in that view of the matter, granting injunction in favour of the plaintiff cannot be sustained.
